s01.slug: MONDAY · 8:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK
body: The Fishbowl TV is on CNN with the sound down to a murmur, and in Berlin it’s ten to six and already dark. The Brandenburg Gate is lit gold, and running away from it along the line where the Wall used to stand is a mile of giant foam dominoes, each one taller than a man and painted by schoolkids from everywhere — a dove, a Trabant, a fist, a sun in sunglasses. Every one of them is still standing. The crawl says somebody gives the first one a shove tonight, Berlin time. In California that’s late morning. Jack will be sitting in a lecture hall when the twentieth century falls over again.
Priya catches him between the front desk and the door. She has her clipboard flat against her chest and, held out at arm’s length in her other hand, a pink envelope.
“Housing sends RAs the hold list,” she says, “and I’m supposed to *facilitate a conversation*.” She puts it in his hand. “This is me facilitating.”

body.title: RESIDENTIAL SERVICES — NOTICE OF BALANCE DUE
body.text:
SPRING 2010 HOUSING · COSTIGAN, JOHN A. · DELGADO 412
Balance after aid: $340.00
A REGISTRATION HOLD has been placed on your record. Payment or an approved arrangement is due at Residential Services by 5:00 p.m., Friday, November 13.

body: “They make it *pink*?”
“Nobody throws away pink,” says Priya. “There were studies.”
Jack knows what three hundred and forty dollars is: the family share, the line on last spring’s aid letter that was supposed to come from Glenwood Avenue and didn’t.

Priya is still going. Freshman registration opens Monday the sixteenth at seven a.m., and a hold means he can’t; Hale’s spring seminar fills by seven-oh-five. “I watched it happen last year from the circulation desk. A sophomore cried on the returns cart.” She checks something on the clipboard that may or may not concern him. “Unrelated. Circulation lost two overnight people to the swine flu. Midnight to six. Eight-forty an hour. I’m not *recommending* it. I’m informing you it exists.”
“Thanks, Priya.”
“That wasn’t a conversation,” she says, already writing. “I’m logging it as one.”

He takes the stairs back up to four for his bag. Somebody has propped the lounge door with a chair, and over the weekend Margot has wiped the whiteboard to the frame and lettered it fresh in her square black capitals:

body.title: THE WHITEBOARD, 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body.text:
20 YEARS · WHO BROUGHT IT DOWN?
(DISCUSS. ARGUE. BE WRONG.)
TONIGHT 9 P.M.
In the corner the useful-idiots tally: C 8 · B 7, and under it, in Margot’s smallest capitals, STUPAK: SAME SIDE (BOTH).

body: In 412 the blinds are down and Theo is asleep on his face with one bare foot off the mattress. Jack finds Hale’s reader on the desk and opens it to the page where he quit last night. He lays the pink envelope in along the spine, creases it once with his thumb so the corner won’t show, and folds the reader shut on it.

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists.

body.text: → Jack Costigan: mom sent u something!!! newman desk. DONT OPEN IT WITHOUT ME

body: Jack reads it at half past four on the Dell with his bag still on his shoulder, and types *I won’t* under it, and posts it. By the time he has the bag off, two people like that too.

Theo comes in behind him with a paper cup from the UCen and *Variety* rolled under his arm, looking for somewhere to set the cup down, and what he settles on is Hale’s reader on the corner of Jack’s desk. The reader is fatter on one side than the other. The cup tips. Theo saves the cup, and the pink envelope slides out across the blotter and stops against his wrist.
Theo never looks for anything. Things present themselves to Theo. He reads this one upside down without picking it up.
“How much?”
“Doesn’t matter.”
Theo turns it right way up with one finger. “Costigan. I spend that on *parking*.”
“You spend that on parking because you park in the fire lane.”
“I park where the light is good.” He waits.
“No,” Jack says.
“You’re the only man I know who’s proud of being broke. It’s very Steinbeck.”
“Steinbeck got paid.”
“Steinbeck had a *publisher*, Costigan. You have me.” He waits again, longer. Jack goes on unlacing his boots.

Theo looks at him for as long as the espresso machine on the shelf takes to tick twice. Then he slides the envelope back into the reader at the same page and lines the reader up with the corner of the desk, exactly where it was, until its edge and the desk’s edge are one edge, and takes his hand away.
“The offer has no expiration date.”

He carries his coffee to his bed and lies down on top of the duvet in his loafers with *Variety* held open over his face. The espresso machine ticks as it cools. Every so often Theo turns a page, sooner than anybody could have read it.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 1:04 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The RAZR lights up on the desk at 1:02 and shivers against Hale’s reader, and the little outside screen says MOM.

Theo doesn’t stir. Jack takes the phone out to the east stairwell in his socks, the Carhartt over his T-shirt, and climbs to the third step above the fourth-floor landing, where the one bar lives, and holds the RAZR up toward the sprinkler head. “Ma.”

It’s four in the morning on Glenwood Avenue, and his mother is very calm. Maria Costigan yells about the cardoons and the Browns and the price of stamps; she goes calm for hospitals and wakes. He sits down on the step, the concrete cold through his socks, and puts his free hand over his other ear against the fluorescent hum. “Okay,” he says. “Okay. Tell me.”

The SUB pay ended last week, she says — the last check. She didn’t tell him, because what was he going to do about it from California. Tonight his father went down to the bar on Midlothian for the Monday game, the Steelers in Denver — “and he doesn’t even *like* the Steelers, Jack” — and the bar closed at two-thirty. It’s after four. The truck isn’t back. His cell phone is on the counter by the toaster; she knows because she called it, and it rang in the kitchen.

Nonna is at the kitchen table with her rosary. She went dizzy on the stairs Sunday and has slept in the chair in the front room since, but tonight she won’t go to the chair. Gina is up too, on the landing, where she thinks nobody can see her.
“I’m not calling the police on your father, Jack,” his mother says. “I’m calling you.”

choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You prayed the Sorrowful Mysteries with her until the truck pulled in.
response: “Let’s pray it, Ma.”

It’s already Tuesday in Youngstown, which makes them the Sorrowful Mysteries. She has her beads out by the time he’s said so; he can hear them on the tabletop. The Agony in the Garden. Partway into the second decade Nonna comes in from the other side of the kitchen in Italian, a syllable behind them and sure of every word — *Santa Maria, Madre di Dio* — and nobody corrects anybody. They’re on the Crowning with Thorns when it comes.

At 4:51 Eastern — nine minutes to two here, the stairwell bright and empty around him — his mother stops in the middle of a word. Headlights, across her kitchen window. Then, down the line from twenty-four hundred miles, a hollow bang and the long rattle of a trash can rolling at the curb, and the Silverado’s bad muffler, and the engine cut.
“He’s home,” she says. “Go to sleep, honey.” And then, because it has been on her list since August: “The spring thing. For your room. We’ll find it.”
“I’ve got it, Ma.”

She goes out with the cordless. He hears the storm door, and the cold of the driveway coming into the phone, and his father’s voice, too low for words, and the storm door again. When she comes back on, she says it quietly. “He sat in the lot at Lordstown. The employee lot. He wanted to see if the lights were on.”

choices.text: Talk to her about anything else.
choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You talked her through it — Rosie’s crabs, the cardoons — until the truck pulled in.
response: So he talks. He asks if Rosie is still drawing crabs, and she is; there’s one on the refrigerator in a hat, his mother reports, on its way to Mass. He asks about the cardoons for Thanksgiving and gets the whole cardoon situation in the Mahoning Valley, which is dire. He asks whether the girl who writes on cows has written again, and his mother says not since the last one, and the last one is in the drawer with the good scissors. Somewhere in the cardoons she laughs once, tired, at herself. He keeps her going.

choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You asked what he said before he left: “Don’t wait up.”
response: “Ma. What did he say before he left?”

Something goes down on the table on Glenwood Avenue — a spoon, a cup. “He said, ‘Don’t wait up.’” She says it in his father’s voice without meaning to. “Twenty-six years, Jack, and he has never said that to me.”
After that they talk about nothing much, and he stays on.

s05a.slug: TUESDAY · 2:06 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, THE LANDING WINDOW
body: The landing window is open its six inches. Below it one sodium lamp lights the Lagoon path orange, the light lying along the asphalt in a single long smear, and nothing on the path moves.
Jack sits on the sill with his back against the frame and the phone shut in his hand. In Youngstown it’s after five in the morning, and he doesn’t know which room his father is asleep in.

The pack of Reds is in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, where it lives. He takes it out and holds it on his knee, the cellophane catching the orange. Four left. He turns it end over end, once, and decides nothing about it at all.
Past the path the eucalyptus stand in the orange light without a leaf moving.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · MISSION STREET POST OFFICE
body: The Mission Street post office has one window open and a line to the door, and the radio behind the counter is playing this morning’s memorial from Fort Hood over again, low — a bugle, then the President. Nobody in line talks.

Jack waits with Hale’s reader in his bag and, in his front pocket, the fold of tip money he’s been keeping back for Friday. At the window he asks for a money order, twenty dollars, and fills in PAY TO from memory — D. KOSTELNIK, STRUTHERS, OH — and leaves FROM blank. Twenty-one ten with the fee. He counts it out of the fold: singles, a five gone limp, a dime. The clerk tears off the customer’s receipt and slides it across, and Jack drops the envelope in the slot marked OUT OF TOWN.
Outside, Rafi Ochoa is sitting on the curb with his skateboard rocking under one heel and a flat-rate box on his knees, addressed in fat felt-pen capitals to OXNARD.
“Boss.” He lifts the box. “My other abuela. My mom’s mom. She gets a box when the first one gets a box. It’s a cold war. I’m just the mailman.”
His eyes touch the receipt in Jack’s hand and go back to the street. “No stress, boss,” he says, though Jack hasn’t said anything.

Then: “I saw Priya get you at the front desk yesterday. With the pink.” A shrug. “Pink’s money. Everybody knows pink.” The board rolls forward and back under his heel. “You need work? I got an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.”
Jack looks at him.

“Vitamins, boss.” Rafi shows both palms, the box balanced on his knees. “Not bars. I don’t do bars.” He holds out a hand for something to write on, and the only paper Jack has is the receipt. Rafi turns it over on his thigh and writes his number on the back in ballpoint, ten digits with a little wave drawn under them, and hands it back.
“Marcus Aurelius says what stands in the way becomes the way,” he says, getting up. “Pretty sure he meant rent.”
He tucks the box under his arm and carries it inside to stand in the line. Jack puts the receipt in his wallet behind the Mooney ID, with the other two.

journal.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)
journal.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike on the wharf at one in the morning like it was nothing, till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says. Outside the post office he offered me an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 5:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE NEWMAN LOUNGE
body: At half past five the Newman lounge is lit by two lamps and the Coke machine, and through the window the olive in the courtyard has gone black against the last green of the sky. Somebody has left a guitar on the couch, and a Bible study’s worth of Styrofoam cups.

The box is on the coffee table — Priority Mail, COEUR D’ALENE ID in the postmark, taped on every seam twice. Becca is kneeling beside it with Mrs. Fitch’s good scissors, which Mrs. Fitch lent her personally, and she has been waiting, because there is an order to this, and the order is that he watches.

She opens it. On top is a letter on the cow stationery, Holsteins grazing up the margins, in Mrs. Lindell’s upright hand, and Becca reads it to him. *Dear Jack, Becca tells me you are her boyfriend now, which we knew. Please find enclosed.* There’s a good deal after that about the weather in Rathdrum and a heifer with opinions, and the word *boyfriend* comes up twice more, and each time Becca reads it a little faster.
Then a tin of molasses cookies with wax paper between the layers. Then a pair of gray wool socks so thick they stand up on their own.
“North Idaho socks,” Becca says.
“Becca. My feet are in *California*.”
“That’s what they’re for.”

At the bottom, wrapped in the *Coeur d’Alene Press*, two jars of huckleberry jam, purple-black, with masking-tape labels in her mother’s Sharpie. One says JACK. The other says FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE.
“Mom thinks everybody’s Catholic till proven otherwise,” Becca says.
“Theo’s been proven otherwise in several jurisdictions.”

He moves Hale’s reader to make room for the jars, and the reader falls open, and the pink envelope slides out across the table and fetches up against the cookie tin. Becca picks it up and reads it with her finger under the line, the way she’d read the tag in a calf’s ear, and her finger stops at HOLD.
“I have six hundred and twelve dollars,” she says. “From Daisy. She was a very good heifer.”

She sold Daisy at the Kootenai County Fair in August of last year and put it in the credit union in Coeur d’Alene and hasn’t touched it, because it was for something that mattered. She explains all of this with his envelope in her hand. There is nothing in her face but the offer.

choices.text: Take her hand. “Keep Daisy. I mean it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You took her hand and told her to keep Daisy.
response: He takes her hand across the box — marker on the knuckles, a nick healing on one of them — and says it. “Keep Daisy. I mean it.”
Becca looks down at their hands, and up at him, and nods once. “Okay,” she says, and keeps hold of him. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

In 412 that night Theo receives the second jar on his feet. He reads the label, holds the jar up to the desk lamp so the light comes through it purple, and inclines his head in the general direction of Idaho. “Tell Mrs. Lindell I’m a supporter, not a member.” He shelves it beside the espresso machine, label out, next to the jar from his birthday.

choices.text: “I can’t accept a cow. My mother would hear about it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You told her you couldn’t accept a cow.
response: “I can’t accept a cow,” he says. “My mother would hear about it.”

Becca laughs out loud, and then she gets serious about it, because she takes his mother seriously. “She’d be proud of you. Daisy was a good cow.” She folds the envelope along its crease and hands it back. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

He reads the label, holds the jar up to the desk lamp so the light comes through it purple, and inclines his head in the general direction of Idaho. “Tell Mrs. Lindell I’m a supporter, not a member.” He shelves it beside the espresso machine, label out, next to the jar from his birthday.

choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You told her straight: you can’t take her heifer.
response: “I can’t take your heifer, Becca.”

She hears it out and nods, weighing it on its merits. “Okay. That’s a real answer.” She folds the envelope along its crease and slides it back into Hale’s reader for him. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 9:40 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE DISH PIT
body: The Hobart runs its cycle with a long rising gargle and a thump, and under it Rudy’s transistor is on KNX, a man reading the traffic on the 405 to a kitchen three hours north of it.

Jack racks coffee cups and tells Rudy about Rafi’s offer as a bit — one ride, two hundred dollars, Rafi’s abuela must run a very tight ship. Rudy doesn’t turn around from the flat-top. He works the scraper in long, even strokes toward the trough.
“I know what an errand is, mijo.”
Jack tries a second one, about Rafi’s abuela and the Marcus Aurelius, and Rudy lets it go by like the KNX weatherman. He doesn’t say anything else for an hour.

Gloria comes back from the walk-in with a crate of lemons on her hip, sets it on the steel, and counts the tip jar at the pass into little towers of quarters. Hale’s reader is on the shelf over the dish station where Jack’s bag lives, the pink corner sticking out of it. Gloria reaches up without asking, tugs the corner out far enough to read the number, and tucks it back.
“I can front you against December, hon,” she says to the quarters. “Don’t tell Rudy. He’ll want one.”
“No, Gloria. Thank you.”
She looks at him over her glasses. Then she sweeps the towers into an envelope and lets him.
At two minutes past ten the RAZR goes off in his apron, and goes off again, and keeps going.

Ashley Vrabel’s father’s DUI. Jack never handed her that. She found it herself.

body: He runs a rack of plates through with the phone face down on the steel. When he comes back to it there’s one more.

body: Jack stands at the sink with the sprayer running on nothing. He heard it too, from the third step of a stairwell twenty-four hundred miles off. He shuts the water off. Behind him Gloria is halving lemons with the big knife, steady as a clock, not looking over.

choices.text: “Apologize to her. Not for the truth. For why you said it.”
response: He types it on T9 with wet thumbs, a letter at a time — *apologize to her. not for the truth. for why u said it* — and it takes him most of a rack.
*good. now never do it again.*

choices.text: “I know about Dad. Ma called me. You’re not carrying it, G.”
choices.key: Gina heard Dad’s truck hit the can. You told her you know, and she isn’t carrying it.
response: *i know about dad. ma called me. ur not carrying it g.*
Four minutes go by on the clock over the pass. Rudy turns a row of patties. Gloria cuts lemons into wheels.

choices.text: Set the alarm for 3:50 and call her before school.
response: He doesn’t text back. He sets the RAZR’s alarm for 3:50, finishes the shift, sleeps three hours in his clothes, and at ten to four he’s on the third step of the east stairwell, where the bar is.

It’s ten to seven on Glenwood Avenue. Gina picks up like she was already holding it. She says *hey*, and *yeah*, and *i guess* — lowercase, somehow, out loud — and he talks to her through a bowl of Cheerios he can hear her eating, and she doesn’t hang up until the bus.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 1:10 AM · THE ANCHOR, UNDER THE HOBART
body: Ten past one on Thursday morning and the Anchor’s kitchen is down to the hum of the walk-in and Rudy scraping the flat-top for the last time tonight. Jack is on his knees on the rubber mat with his arm under the Hobart to the shoulder.
The Folgers can comes out with a skin of grease-dust on the lid. He counts it once, on the mat, in the light from the pass.

body.text: One hundred fifty-four dollars. The ANCHOR envelope is in a St. Vincent de Paul basket, and that’s where it should be.
body.else: It isn’t three hundred and forty dollars. It isn’t close.

body.text: *Your penance is to let somebody help you this week.* It’s Thursday.

body: The hold is due tomorrow at five. Registration opens Monday at seven. Daisy is in a credit union in Coeur d’Alene, where she belongs, and Gloria’s offer went into an envelope with the quarters.

He takes out his wallet. Behind the Mooney ID, three stubs, and on the back of the newest, Rafi’s number with its little wave. On the fourth floor of Delgado, Theo is awake; Theo is always awake. Across the Commons the Brick’s circulation desk is short two people, and Priya is behind it.

The kitchen smells of bleach water and the last of the bacon. The walk-in hums. Rudy scrapes, and doesn’t ask what Jack is doing on the floor with a coffee can. Rudy did six years at Soledad. He has seen men count money on a floor before.

choices.text: Call Rafi. One ride, two hundred.
choices.key: Thursday you ran Rafi’s errand. Two hundred dollars, folded once.
response: Rafi picks up on the second ring with the sea somewhere behind him. “Thursday, boss. Two o’clock, behind Delgado. Bring La Flaca.” At the flat-top, Rudy’s scraper stops, and then starts again.

choices.text: Let Theo. It goes on the tab.
choices.key: You let Theo pay the hold. It’s on the tab.

response.text: Residential Services, 9:00 AM. Bring photo ID. I have a form.

body: The harbor at a quarter past two is hard white glare off flat water, and on the bait-dock float the sea lions are asleep in a heap, one of them complaining in its sleep.

The Vans shoebox rides in La Flaca’s basket, taped shut along every edge with blue painter’s tape. It is heavier than shoes. Rafi set it in the basket behind Delgado at two o’clock and said, “Back door of the Wharf Rat. Knock twice. Don’t open it, boss. It’s not your birthday.” Jack coasts down Mission with the coaster brake ticking and the box jumping at every seam in the road.
Ray Ochoa comes out of the Anchor as he’s passing it, a coffee to go in one hand and his windbreaker over the other arm, and Jack has to stop for him or hit him.
“Saint Isidore.” Ray’s eyes go to the basket and come back up. “New shoes?”
“My roommate’s.”

“Big feet, your roommate.” Ray blows across the lid of his coffee and looks out at the sea lions for a while. Then he walks off up the wharf toward Anacapa Street, toward the station, with his coffee.

The Wharf Rat’s back door is in the alley behind the bait shop, propped open on a mop bucket. Jack knocks twice on the frame. A man in a Raiders cap takes the shoebox, weighs it in his hands without looking at it, and gives him back two hundred dollars in twenties, folded once. “Rafi says gracias.” The door swings to against the bucket.

At 3:55, at the Residential Services window, Jack puts two kinds of money on the counter: a hundred and forty out of the Folgers can, in fives and singles that smell like coffee, and Rafi’s twenties, crisp, smelling of nothing. The clerk counts them twice and types, and somewhere in the system a hold lets go.

Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. The hold’s paid. A hundred forty out of the can and two hundred from Rafi’s errand. A shoebox to the Wharf Rat’s back door.

journal.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)
journal.text: Detective Sergeant, per the badge wallet. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter: Tuesdays, meatloaf, a nod to Rudy. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property. Thursday on the wharf: ‘Saint Isidore. New shoes?’ He didn’t look in the box.

s11b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:05 AM · RESIDENTIAL SERVICES, THE WINDOW
body: Residential Services opens at nine, and at five past Theo Vance is at the window in a navy blazer. On Theo, a blazer at nine in the morning means an event.
“Poppy has a recital,” he says. “La Cañada. I’m expected in the front row by two.”
The clerk wears her reading glasses on a beaded chain, and when Theo hands over his card she holds it up to the fluorescent light, and turns it over, and holds it up again.
“It’s real,” Theo tells her. “It’s just very ugly.”
She runs it. The machine thinks about it and prints. She looks at the slip, then at Theo, then at the blazer, and seems to reach some private conclusion about the state of higher education.
Jack is beside him with his wallet half out and his argument ready.
“It’s not charity, Costigan,” Theo says, signing. “It’s an investment in my roommate situation. I’ve seen the alternatives. One of them has a ferret.”
“It goes on the tab.”
“There is no tab.”
“There’s a tab, Theo.”
Theo sighs at the ceiling tiles, takes the receipt from the clerk, turns it over on the counter, and writes on the back in small square capitals, holding the ballpoint like a fountain pen:
He hands it over. “The pie is non-negotiable. It’s how I’ll know you’re sincere.”

Jack puts the wallet back in his pocket. He knows what this is. Somebody is helping him, and his part is to stand still for it, and he would honestly rather do the Stations of the Cross on his knees up the Delgado stairs.
Theo is already at the door, checking the Submariner. “Peach, Costigan. Not a cobbler. A pie.”

Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. The hold’s paid. Theo, at the window, in a blazer. The tab: $340.00, plus one pie (peach).

body: At nine sharp Priya is standing with her back to the Residential Services door while a student worker unlocks it from inside, holding to her chest a form in a laminated sleeve. She has not slept. She has the look of someone who considers this a choice she made correctly.
“Hardship extension,” she says. “Per Section 4.2. I filled it out.”
She has: his name, his student ID, his room, his mother’s maiden name for reasons the form does not explain, and the rest in her smallest print.

body.title: RESIDENTIAL SERVICES — REQUEST FOR HARDSHIP EXTENSION (RS-12)
body.text:
STUDENT: COSTIGAN, JOHN A. · DELGADO 412
AMOUNT: $340.00 · CURRENT DUE DATE: 11/13/09
REQUESTED DUE DATE: 12/01/09, pending campus payroll (Pacifica Library, Circulation, night)
DESCRIBE THE HARDSHIP: Documented.
RA SIGNATURE: P. Raman, 401

body: “How did you document it?”
“You texted me at the circulation desk at one in the morning, Jack. That’s documentation.”

The clerk reads it, and stamps it, and the hold slides to December first, pending payroll. The night desk at the Brick is tonight and Friday, midnight to six, eight-forty an hour; Priya has put him on the schedule already, in pencil.

“I’ll want the sleeve back,” she says. “The sleeves are mine. I buy them by the hundred at the Staples on Mission, and Housing has not reimbursed me one time, and I’ve stopped asking, because asking would mean filling out a form, and I won’t be made to fill out a form to get reimbursed for the sleeves I put forms in.”
Jack thinks about that, and decides it’s airtight.
“Priya. Thank you.”

“It’s a form.” She looks at the stamp, not at him. “Forms are how people help each other without anybody having to look at anybody.” Then she does look at him, over the clipboard. “Don’t make me regret informing you.”

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Filled out my hardship form before I asked. Laminated. She wants the sleeve back.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 10:32 PM · MISSION STREET → THE 11 BUS
body: On the sidewalk outside Bastille the string lights are still on and the chalkboard has been turned to face the wall. Julian comes out last with his guitar case, and stops beside Lena, and asks it gently, as if he were asking permission for something much smaller. “Can I walk you back?”
“Yes,” Lena says.
“Lovely set, Julian,” says Laney, perfectly polite. Her pink BlackBerry is in her hand, and it stays dark.

The 11 comes up Mission at twenty to eleven, nearly empty. Jack and Laney take the long back seat. Lena and Julian sit three rows up, a guitar case’s width between them, the case standing upright in the aisle with his hand on its neck. Laney rides down Ocean Road with her chin on the seatback in front of her and her eyes on the backs of their heads.

At the Anacapa stop Lena and Julian get off first. Laney waits until they’re on the path, then hooks her arm through Jack’s and steers him the other way, round the far side of the Lagoon, into the dark along the water.
“Walk me home, fireman,” she says. “Apparently I’m available.”
Across the black water, far ahead, the door of Delgado opens its rectangle of light with two shapes standing in it, and then the light narrows to a line, and the line goes out.

body.text: The Brick, 11:55, the night desk: a returns cart; three grad students asleep on their arms; at 1:45 the lights blink once for the custodians. Eight-forty an hour, and nobody asks him anything.
body.else: Across the Commons the Brick’s second floor is lit, as it is every night.
